title.narrative: Stöd till Save the Childrens landstrategi för Afghanistan 2022-2025
Support to Save the Children's country strategy for Afghanistan 2022-2025

description.narrative:
Objective of the intervention and expectations of achievements
SCI-Af's vision: is a world in which every child attains the right to survival, protection, development and participation.
SCI-Af's mission: to inspire breakthroughs in the way the world treats children and achieve immediate and lasting change in their lives.
Three breakthroughs until 2030 have been identified: SURVIVE (no child dies preventable causes before 5th birthday), LEARN (All children learn from a quality basic education), BE PROTECTED (Violence against children is no longer tolerated).
The two strategic goals this intervention will aim to reach are:
1. Boys and girls have continuous access to safe and inclusive learning opportunities.
2. Boys and girls enjoy strengthened protective environment and improved social, physical, and emotional well-being.
Insatsen är ett programstöd till Save the Children för implementering av landstrategin men fokus på barns rätt och skydd av barn, utbildningsinsatser i byar samt familjers försörjning.
The contribution is program support to Save the Children's country strategy in Afghanistan with focus on child protection and child rights, community based education and livelihoods.

Results from the entire programme 2022-2025
Strategic Goal 1 Education: Key Results and Behavioural Change
Outcome 1.1. Children gained sustained access to safe, inclusive learning
- 95% retention in Community Based Education (CBE) classes across the programme period. 95% of crisisaffected children remained in school throughout the whole project period.
- Over 12,000 children supported in 2022; 10,820 in 2023; 8,268 in 2024.
- Thousands transitioned to formal school (e.g., 3,217 in 2022; 1,558 in 2023).
Behavioural change among children
Children reported feeling safe, supported, and respected:
"In this CBE class, I dont feel afraid anymore My teachers are nice and care about our needs." (Girl, Kabul)
This indicates increased trust in learning environments, improved emotional wellbeing, and stronger motivation to attend school.
Outcome 1.2. Teachers improved teaching quality and child centred practices
- Teachers trained in Psycho-social support, Social and Emotional Learning, Psychological First Aid, Safe Identification and Referral, and subject knowledge.
- Regular mentoring by master trainers strengthened classroom practice.
Behavioural change among teachers
Teachers adopted nonviolent, supportive approaches:
"The teacher never punished or resorted to violence Its a good place to learn." (Boy, Jawzjan)
This reflects a shift toward positive discipline, safer classrooms, and better learning outcomes.
Outcome 1.3. Communities became active supporters of education
- Community Education Committees and Shuras met 24 times per month to monitor attendance, safety, and teacher performance.
- Communities helped reduce absenteeism, rehabilitate classrooms, and advocate for girls education.
Behavioural change among communities
Parents and elders increasingly supported girls education:
- Parents became more supportive of their childrens education, especially girls.
- Communities also requested additional CBE classes, showing strong ownership.
Strategic Goal 2 Child Protection: Key Results and Behavioural Change
Outcome 2.1. Communitybased child protection systems strengthened
- 100 Community Based Child Protection Networks strengthened (1,000 members).
- Members trained in child rights, Psycological First Aid, Safe Identification Referral, Mental Health and Psycho-Social Support, gender from an Islamic perspective.
- 15,371 community members participated in Mental Health and Psycho-Social Support dialogues.
Behavioural change among community actors
Community Based Child Protection Networks (CBCPN):
Prevented child marriages, Reenrolled children in school, Convinced parents to stop physical punishment and Intervened in child labour cases
Many CBCPN members changed harmful practices at the family level before spreading the message.
This shows internalisation of child protection norms.
Outcome 2.2. Case management and referral systems improved
- 1,813 children received individualised case management (target: 1,712).
- Children received support for abuse, neglect, child labour, and health issues.
- 1,332 children obtained National ID cards (NID), enabling access to services.
Behavioural change among families
Families increasingly sought help and accepted referrals, reflecting growing trust in protection services.
Outcome 2.3. Coordination among child protection actors strengthened
Save the Children International Afghanistan coled the Child Protection Area of Responsibility, improving:
- Service mapping
- Referral pathways
- Case management standards (CPIMS)
- Advocacy with Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (MoLSA)
Behavioural change among authorities
The de facto authorities representatives showed:
- Increased understanding of child protection
- Greater acceptance of communitybased approaches
- Support for establishing a department for girls and womens affairs within MoLSA
This marks a shift in institutional attitudes.
Outcome 2.4. Children accessed safe spaces and resilience programmes
- 4,843 children enrolled in Child-Friendly Space (target: 4,600).
- 3,234 adolescents participated in Youth Resilience Programme.
- 3,217 children reached through the Shabnam & Shadab modality.
- 2,852 children attended Community Children Centres (target: 1,700).
Behavioural change among children
Children demonstrated:
- Improved emotional regulation Increased confidence Better communication and conflictresolution skills
Parents confirmed these changes:
Our children have learned a lot we have seen them grow in their reading, writing, and math skills.
Outcome 2.5. Families adopted positive parenting and genderequitable practices
- 4,694 parents/caregivers trained (target: 4,169).
- Safe Families and Fatherhood modules reduced harmful discipline.
Behavioural change among parents
Parents reported:
- Reduced physical punishment
- Improved communication
- More equitable gender attitudes
- Stronger emotional bonds with children
Parents acknowledged past harmful practices and expressed commitment to changing these behaviours.
Fathers began sharing household responsibilities and adopting nonviolent parenting.
Outcome 2.6. Children meaningfully participated in protection and community decisionmaking
- 5,047 children participated in Child Led Participatory Situation Analysis (target: 4,600).
- Children identified risks such as violence, unsafe water, child labour, and school access barriers.
- Their recommendations shaped CBCPN action plans and Civil Society Organisation initiatives.
Behavioural change among children and adults
Children became active agents of change, and adults increasingly valued childrens voices:
- District Child Protection Action Network repaired a bridge after children highlighted safety risks.
- Communities acted on childrens concerns about violence and discrimination.
Other results
Integrated Community Children Centre (CCC) Modality Transformative Results
The CCC model combined education, protection, livelihoods, and parenting support.
Key results
- 2,030 children and families supported in Kabul and other provinces.
- Catchup classes improved literacy and numeracy.
- Income Generating Activities and multi-purpose cash assistance reduced reliance on child labour.
- Parenting sessions strengthened family relationships.
Behavioural change
- Families shifted from child labour to schooling.
- The de facto authorities strongly supported the CCC model, enabling scaleup.
- Children gained confidence, safety, and learning opportunities.
Summary: What Changed as a result of the Programme?
Across all outcomes, the programme produced tangible, measurable results and deep behavioural change:
Children
Felt safer, more confident, and more emotionally resilient Improved literacy, numeracy, and social skills Became active participants in community decisionmaking
Parents & Caregivers
Adopted positive parenting Reduced physical punishment Supported girls education Improved household economy, reducing child labour
Teachers
Shifted to childcentred, nonviolent teaching Improved subject knowledge and psychosocial support skills
Communities
Took ownership of education and protection structures Actively prevented child marriage and child labour Advocated for more CBE classes and girls education
Authorities (DFA)
Increased acceptance of child protection Supported CCC modality Improved coordination with NGOs Approved a national MoU for child protection (2025)
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
